```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4
)
```

`gt_openadmixture()` estimates individual ancestry proportions (Q) and
ancestral allele frequencies (P) under the ADMIXTURE model, using the
algorithm of OpenADMIXTURE.jl (Ko et al. 2023), reimplemented in C++ within
`tidygenclust` (no Julia or Python needed). It works directly on the backing files of
`tidypopgen` `gen_tibble` objects, and returns `gt_admix` objects that can be
explored and plotted with the methods provided by `tidypopgen`.

In this vignette, we use the dataset of the lizard *Anolis punctatus* from
Prates et al. (2018), the same example used in `tidypopgen` and in the main
`tidygenclust` vignette, and compare our results with those of the original
ADMIXTURE program.

# Read the data

We read the vcf file of the 46 lizards into a `gen_tibble`, add the
population information, and group the individuals by population:

```{r}
library(tidypopgen)
library(tidygenclust)

vcf_path <- system.file(
  "/extdata/anolis/punctatus_t70_s10_n46_filtered.recode.vcf.gz",
  package = "tidypopgen"
)
anole_gt <- gen_tibble(vcf_path,
  quiet = TRUE, backingfile = tempfile("anolis_"),
  parser = "cpp"
)
pops_path <- system.file("/extdata/anolis/punctatus_n46_meta.csv",
  package = "tidypopgen"
)
pops <- utils::read.csv(pops_path)
anole_gt <- anole_gt %>%
  left_join(pops, by = "id") %>%
  group_by(population)
anole_gt
```

The data include missing genotypes:

```{r}
mean(is.na(show_genotypes(anole_gt)))
```

`gt_openadmixture()` simply ignores missing genotypes when computing the
likelihood, so there is no need to impute them first.

# Run gt_openadmixture()

We estimate ancestry for K = 2 to 4, with 3 runs for each value of K, each
run starting from a different random seed:

```{r}
seeds <- c(42, 2, 16)
time_oa <- system.time(
  anole_oa <- gt_openadmixture(anole_gt,
    k = 2:4, n_runs = 3, seed = seeds
  )
)
time_oa
summary(anole_oa)
```

The results are stored in a `gt_admix` object, so we can use all the methods
from `tidypopgen`. For example, we can plot the run with the highest
log-likelihood for K = 3:

```{r}
best_run <- function(adm, k) {
  runs <- which(adm$k == k)
  which.max(adm$loglik[runs])
}
autoplot(anole_oa,
  type = "barplot", k = 3, run = best_run(anole_oa, 3),
  annotate_group = TRUE
)
```

Our three clusters correspond to the three genetic groups found by Prates et
al. (2018): Eastern Amazonia, Western Amazonia and the Atlantic Forest.

We can extract the Q matrix of a given run, and use `augment()` to add it to
the `gen_tibble`:

```{r}
q_mat <- get_q_matrix(anole_oa, k = 3, run = best_run(anole_oa, 3))
augment(q_mat, data = anole_gt) %>%
  select(id, population, pop, .Q1, .Q2, .Q3) %>%
  head()
```

The P matrices give the frequency of the alternate allele of each locus
(`allele_alt` in `show_loci()`) in each ancestral population:

```{r}
head(get_p_matrix(anole_oa, k = 3, run = best_run(anole_oa, 3)))
```

# Comparison with ADMIXTURE

We now compare `gt_openadmixture()` with the original ADMIXTURE program
(Alexander et al. 2009), run through `tidypopgen::gt_admixture()`. The
easiest way to get ADMIXTURE is with `tgc_tools_install()`, which creates a
conda environment, `ctidygenclust`, containing ADMIXTURE (and the other
tools used by `tidygenclust`):

```{r, eval = FALSE}
tgc_tools_install()
```

The rest of this section is only run if this conda environment is available:

```{r}
admixture_available <- tryCatch(
  "ctidygenclust" %in% reticulate::conda_list()$name,
  error = function(e) FALSE
)
admixture_available
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = admixture_available)
```

We run ADMIXTURE with the same values of K, number of runs and seeds:

```{r}
time_adm <- system.time(
  anole_adm <- gt_admixture(anole_gt,
    k = 2:4, n_runs = 3, seed = seeds,
    conda_env = "ctidygenclust"
  )
)
time_adm
```

## Speed

On this small dataset, both programs are fast, but `gt_openadmixture()`
avoids writing PLINK files and starting an external program for each run:

```{r}
data.frame(
  method = c("gt_openadmixture", "ADMIXTURE"),
  elapsed_seconds = c(time_oa[["elapsed"]], time_adm[["elapsed"]])
)
```

The advantage grows with the size of the dataset; on the 379 individuals and
54,051 SNPs of the `EUR_subset` data used to test OpenADMIXTURE.jl (K = 4,
4 cores), `gt_openadmixture()` took 19 seconds and ADMIXTURE 153 seconds,
reaching log-likelihoods within 1 unit of each other (-15,552,193.2 and
-15,552,192.6).

## Log-likelihoods

Both programs maximise the same likelihood, so their log-likelihoods can be
compared directly:

```{r}
loglik_tbl <- data.frame(
  k = anole_oa$k,
  run = rep(1:3, 3),
  openadmixture = anole_oa$loglik,
  admixture = anole_adm$loglik
)
loglik_tbl$difference <- loglik_tbl$openadmixture - loglik_tbl$admixture
loglik_tbl
```

For a given K, runs started from different seeds end at slightly different
log-likelihoods. This is not a convergence problem: the likelihood surface
of this small dataset has many local optima, and both programs end up in
one of them depending on the starting point. Neither program is
systematically better; comparing the best run of each:

```{r}
best_tbl <- do.call(rbind, lapply(2:4, function(k) {
  data.frame(
    k = k,
    openadmixture = max(anole_oa$loglik[anole_oa$k == k]),
    admixture = max(anole_adm$loglik[anole_adm$k == k])
  )
}))
best_tbl
```

## Ancestry proportions

The labels of the clusters are arbitrary, so to compare Q matrices we first
match each cluster of `gt_openadmixture()` to the most similar cluster of
ADMIXTURE:

```{r}
# all permutations of 1:n
permutations <- function(n) {
  if (n == 1) {
    return(matrix(1))
  }
  sub <- permutations(n - 1)
  do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(n), function(i) {
    cbind(i, matrix(setdiff(seq_len(n), i)[sub], nrow = nrow(sub)))
  }))
}
# reorder the columns of q so that they best match q_ref
match_q <- function(q, q_ref) {
  perms <- permutations(ncol(q))
  diffs <- apply(perms, 1, function(x) sum(abs(q[, x] - q_ref)))
  q[, perms[which.min(diffs), ]]
}
```

For the best run of each method, the ancestry proportions are very similar:

```{r}
q_comparison <- do.call(rbind, lapply(2:4, function(k) {
  q_oa <- unclass(get_q_matrix(anole_oa, k = k, run = best_run(anole_oa, k)))
  q_adm <- unclass(
    get_q_matrix(anole_adm, k = k, run = best_run(anole_adm, k))
  )
  q_oa <- match_q(q_oa, q_adm)
  data.frame(
    k = k,
    mean_abs_difference = mean(abs(q_oa - q_adm)),
    max_abs_difference = max(abs(q_oa - q_adm)),
    correlation = stats::cor(as.vector(q_oa), as.vector(q_adm))
  )
}))
q_comparison
```

We can visualise the comparison for K = 3 by plotting the ancestry
proportions estimated by the two methods against each other:

```{r, fig.width = 5, fig.height = 5}
library(ggplot2)
q_oa <- unclass(get_q_matrix(anole_oa, k = 3, run = best_run(anole_oa, 3)))
q_adm <- unclass(get_q_matrix(anole_adm, k = 3, run = best_run(anole_adm, 3)))
q_oa <- match_q(q_oa, q_adm)
data.frame(
  admixture = as.vector(q_adm),
  openadmixture = as.vector(q_oa),
  cluster = factor(rep(1:3, each = nrow(q_adm)))
) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = admixture, y = openadmixture, colour = cluster)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point() +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "Q (ADMIXTURE)", y = "Q (gt_openadmixture)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

and by comparing the bar plots:

```{r}
autoplot(anole_oa,
  type = "barplot", k = 3, run = best_run(anole_oa, 3),
  annotate_group = TRUE
) +
  ggtitle("gt_openadmixture")
autoplot(anole_adm,
  type = "barplot", k = 3, run = best_run(anole_adm, 3),
  annotate_group = TRUE
) +
  ggtitle("ADMIXTURE")
```

## Allele frequencies

So far we have only compared the Q matrices. Comparing the P matrices needs
care, for two reasons:

1. ADMIXTURE writes its P matrix with the loci sorted by chromosome and
   position, rather than in the order of the input. In current releases of
   `tidypopgen`, `gt_admixture()` does not undo this reordering, so the rows
   of its P matrices do not match the loci of the `gen_tibble` when the loci
   are not already sorted (as is the case for this dataset, whose chromosome
   names are not numeric). A fix (EvolEcolGroup/tidypopgen#211) will soon be
   available in the development version of `tidypopgen`.
2. Even with the rows in the correct order, the two methods report the
   frequency of different alleles: `gt_openadmixture()` gives the frequency
   of the alternate allele (`allele_alt`), whilst ADMIXTURE gives the
   frequency of the second allele in the PLINK bim file, which for a
   `gen_tibble` is the reference allele (`allele_ref`). The P matrices of
   ADMIXTURE therefore need to be flipped before comparing them with those of
   `gt_openadmixture()`:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# with a version of tidypopgen that includes the fix
p_oa <- get_p_matrix(anole_oa, k = 3, run = best_run(anole_oa, 3))
p_adm <- 1 - as.matrix(
  get_p_matrix(anole_adm, k = 3, run = best_run(anole_adm, 3))
)
# columns should first be matched as for the Q matrices
```

# References

Alexander DH, Novembre J, Lange K (2009) Fast model-based estimation of
ancestry in unrelated individuals. Genome Research, 19(9), 1655-1664.

Ko S, Chu BB, Peterson D, Okenwa C, Papp JC, Alexander DH, Sobel EM, Zhou H,
Lange KL (2023) Unsupervised discovery of ancestry informative markers and
genetic admixture proportions in biobank-scale datasets. The American
Journal of Human Genetics, 110(2), 314-325.

Prates I, Penna A, Rodrigues MT, Carnaval AC (2018) Local adaptation in
mainland anole lizards: Integrating population history and genome-environment
associations. Ecology and Evolution, 8(23), 11932-11944.
